text: Prophet is an open-source forecasting library, originally released by Meta, designed for business time series with strong seasonal patterns and holidays. Where ARIMA asks you to pick orders, Prophet asks you to describe the series in business terms: a trend that can bend, repeating weekly and yearly patterns, and optional holidays, fit with a Bayesian model.

Prophet insists on a DataFrame with exactly two columns: a date column called d-s, and a numeric column called y. No index tricks, no frequency setting. You fit it, call make_future_dataframe for the horizon, then predict -- which returns yhat, yhat_lower, yhat_upper, and one column per component.

With defaults, Prophet scored a mean absolute error of twenty-four point two -- worse than the seasonal naive baseline of sixteen point one three. Printing m.seasonalities showed only weekly was fitted. Here's the gotcha: Prophet switches on yearly seasonality only if training history spans at least two years, and ours was just short, at seven hundred two days.

Forcing it with yearly_seasonality equals True dropped the error from twenty-four point two to six point seven one -- better than seasonal naive, and in the same range as Holt-Winters and SARIMA. One argument. Always print m.seasonalities and check the model contains what you believe your series contains.

Holidays add by name or country with add_country_holidays -- our synthetic series has no real holiday effects, so the score barely moved, to six point four eight, which is noise, not signal. On real retail data with genuine holiday spikes, the effect can be large. Prophet also ships a rolling-origin backtest through cross_validation.

Over four cutoffs spaced ninety days apart, each forecasting twenty-eight days out, the backtest's average M.A.E. was seven point three one, consistent with the single window's six point seven one. Prophet refits the model at every cutoff, so a backtest takes noticeably longer than one fit.

Prophet needs a d-s and y DataFrame, then fit, make_future_dataframe, and predict. It models trend, seasonality, and optional holidays. Yearly seasonality is off by default under two years of history -- always check m.seasonalities. Next lesson: forecasting with machine learning, where lags and calendar features feed models you already know.
